public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 987

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/987](https://www.erdosproblems.com/987)
- [APSSV26b] B. Alexeev, M. Putterman, M. Sawhney, M. Sellke, and G. Valiant,
  [Short proofs in combinatorics, probability, and number theory II](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.06609).
  arXiv:2604.06609 (2026).
- [Cl67] Clunie, J., On a problem of Erdős. J. London Math. Soc. (1967), 133--136.
- [Er64b] Erdős, P., Problems and results on diophantine approximations. Compositio Math. (1964),
  52-65.
- [Er65b] Erdős, P., Some remarks on number theory. Israel J. Math. (the actual reference
  cited by Clunie 1967 as [2]; the erdosproblems.com bibliography points to a different
  Erdős 1965 paper, "Some recent advances and current problems in number theory" (Lectures
  on Modern Mathematics III, 1965, 196-244), which does not appear to contain the
  exponential-sum log-bound proof).
- [Ha74] Hayman, W. K., Research problems in function theory: new problems. (1974), 155--180.
- [Li69] Lindström, B., An inequality for $B_2$-sequences. J. Combinatorial Theory (1969), 211-212.
-/

@[expose] public section

open Filter Finset Asymptotics
open scoped ExponentialSum

namespace Erdos987

/-
Here we use 0-indexing for generality and convenience, while in the original problem
formulation 1-indexing was used. This change does not affect the meaning of the problem.
In the description of the problem below we remain faithful to the original one.
-/

/--
For an infinite sequence $x_1, x_2, \ldots \in (0, 1)$, define
$$A_k = \limsup_{n \to \infty} \left\lvert \sum_{j \le n} e(k x_j) \right\rvert,$$
where $e(x) = e^{2\pi i x}$.
-/
noncomputable def A (x : ℕ → ℝ) (k : ℕ) : EReal :=
  atTop.limsup fun n : ℕ => (‖∑ j ∈ range n, e (k * x j)‖ : EReal)

/- ## Question 1 -/

/-- Question 1:

Is it true that $\limsup_{k \to \infty} A_k = \infty$?

Erdős [Er64b] remarks it is "easy to see" that $\limsup_k \sup_n |\sum_{j \le n} e(k x_j)| = \infty$.
Erdős [Er65b] later found a "very easy" proof that $A_k \gg \log k$ for infinitely many $k$.
Clunie [Cl67] proved that $A_k \gg k^{1/2}$ for infinitely many $k$, which implies the answer is
yes (Tao independently found a proof). This is Problem 7.21 in [Ha74]. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11 40 42, formal_proof using lean4 at
"https://github.com/Marti2203/formal-conjectures/blob/19c63d48acce3099c242b059518c49bf8dc0eab8/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/987.lean"]
theorem erdos_987.parts.i :
    answer(True) ↔ ∀ (x : ℕ → ℝ) (_ : ∀ j : ℕ, x j ∈ Set.Ioo (0 : ℝ) 1),
      atTop.limsup (fun k : ℕ => A x k) = ⊤ := by
  sorry

/-- Erdős [Er64b] remarks it is "easy to see" that for every infinite sequence
$x_1, x_2, \ldots \in (0, 1)$,
$$\limsup_{k \to \infty} \sup_n \left\lvert \sum_{j \le n} e(k x_j) \right\rvert = \infty.$$ -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11 40 42, formal_proof using lean4 at
"https://github.com/Marti2203/formal-conjectures/blob/19c63d48acce3099c242b059518c49bf8dc0eab8/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/987.lean"]
theorem erdos_987.variants.sup_limsup_infty
    (x : ℕ → ℝ) (hx : ∀ j : ℕ, x j ∈ Set.Ioo (0 : ℝ) 1) :
    atTop.limsup (fun k : ℕ =>
      ⨆ n : ℕ, ((‖∑ j ∈ range n, e ((k : ℝ) * x j)‖ : ℝ) : EReal)) = ⊤ := by
  sorry

/-- Erdős [Er65b] proved that, for every infinite sequence $x_1, x_2, \ldots \in (0, 1)$,
$A_k \gg \log k$ for infinitely many $k$. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11 40 42, formal_proof using lean4 at
"https://github.com/Marti2203/formal-conjectures/blob/19c63d48acce3099c242b059518c49bf8dc0eab8/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/987.lean"]
theorem erdos_987.variants.log_lower_bound
    (x : ℕ → ℝ) (_hx : ∀ j : ℕ, x j ∈ Set.Ioo (0 : ℝ) 1) :
    ∃ c > 0, ∃ᶠ k : ℕ in atTop, ((c * Real.log k : ℝ) : EReal) ≤ A x k := by
  sorry

/-- Clunie [Cl67] proved that, for every infinite sequence $x_1, x_2, \ldots \in (0, 1)$,
$A_k \gg k^{1/2}$ for infinitely many $k$. (Tao independently found a proof.) -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11 40 42, formal_proof using lean4 at
"https://github.com/Marti2203/formal-conjectures/blob/19c63d48acce3099c242b059518c49bf8dc0eab8/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/987.lean"]
theorem erdos_987.variants.sqrt_lower_bound
    (x : ℕ → ℝ) (hx : ∀ j : ℕ, x j ∈ Set.Ioo (0 : ℝ) 1) :
    ∃ c > 0, ∃ᶠ k : ℕ in atTop, ((c * Real.sqrt k : ℝ) : EReal) ≤ A x k := by
  sorry

/-- **Linear upper bound (weakened).** A first weakened version of Clunie's `A_k ≤ k`: there
exists a sequence $x \in (0,1)$ with $A_k \le 2k$ for all $k \ge 1$. The witness is the
(shifted) van der Corput sequence. For the tighter $A_k \le k + 1$ bound see
`linear_upper_bound_clunie`. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11 40 42, formal_proof using lean4 at
"https://github.com/Marti2203/formal-conjectures/blob/19c63d48acce3099c242b059518c49bf8dc0eab8/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/987.lean"]
theorem erdos_987.variants.linear_upper_bound_weak :
    ∃ (x : ℕ → ℝ) (_ : ∀ j : ℕ, x j ∈ Set.Ioo (0 : ℝ) 1),
      ∀ k : ℕ, 1 ≤ k → A x k ≤ ((2 * k : ℝ) : EReal) := by
  sorry

/-- **Linear upper bound (tight via Clunie phase tracking).** Tighter than
`linear_upper_bound_weak`: there exists a sequence $x \in (0,1)$ with $A_k \le k + 1$ for all
$k \ge 1$, via the (shifted) van der Corput sequence. Whether the $+1$ can be eliminated to
recover Clunie's exact $A_k \le k$ under the strict $\mathrm{Ioo}\,0\,1$ hypothesis is open in
this formalization (see `linear_upper_bound`). -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11 40 42, formal_proof using lean4 at
"https://github.com/Marti2203/formal-conjectures/blob/19c63d48acce3099c242b059518c49bf8dc0eab8/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/987.lean"]
theorem erdos_987.variants.linear_upper_bound_clunie :
    ∃ (x : ℕ → ℝ) (_ : ∀ j : ℕ, x j ∈ Set.Ioo (0 : ℝ) 1),
      ∀ k : ℕ, 1 ≤ k → A x k ≤ (((k : ℝ) + 1) : EReal) := by
  sorry

/-- Clunie [Cl67] proved that there exists an infinite sequence $\{z_\nu\}$ on the unit circle
with $A_\nu \le \nu$ for all $\nu \ge 1$. Translating $z_\nu = e(x_\nu)$, the natural domain of
$x_\nu$ is the half-open unit interval $\mathrm{Ico}\,0\,1$, matching the original
[Er64b]/[Cl67] statement (any unit complex number is allowed, including $z = 1$, i.e. $x = 0$).

**Note**: erdosproblems.com/987 phrases the problem with the *open* interval
$x_\nu \in (0, 1)$, which excludes $z = 1$ and is strictly stronger than what [Er64b]/[Cl67]
state; we align with the original papers here. The shifted-vdc $\le k + 1$ variant under the
open interval is preserved as `linear_upper_bound_clunie`. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11 40 42, formal_proof using lean4 at
"https://github.com/Marti2203/formal-conjectures/blob/19c63d48acce3099c242b059518c49bf8dc0eab8/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/987.lean"]
theorem erdos_987.variants.linear_upper_bound :
    ∃ (x : ℕ → ℝ) (_ : ∀ j : ℕ, x j ∈ Set.Ico (0 : ℝ) 1),
      ∀ k : ℕ, 1 ≤ k → A x k ≤ ((k : ℝ) : EReal) := by
  sorry

/-- An internal OpenAI model (see [APSSV26b, §3]) proved that there exists an infinite sequence
$x_1, x_2, \ldots \in (0, 1)$ such that
$\sup_n \left\lvert \sum_{j \le n} e(k x_j) \right\rvert \ll (k \log k)^{1/2}$ for all $k \ge 1$
(in particular $A_k \ll (k \log k)^{1/2}$).

Note: the bound is restricted to $k \ge 2$ since $\log 1 = 0$ would make the RHS vanish at
$k = 1$, while the LHS $\|\sum_{j < n} e(x_j)\|$ can equal $1$ (e.g. for $n = 1$). -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11 40 42, formal_proof using lean4 at
"https://github.com/Marti2203/formal-conjectures/blob/19c63d48acce3099c242b059518c49bf8dc0eab8/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/987.lean"]
theorem erdos_987.variants.sqrt_log_upper_bound :
    ∃ (x : ℕ → ℝ) (_ : ∀ j : ℕ, x j ∈ Set.Ioo (0 : ℝ) 1) (C : ℝ) (_ : 0 < C),
      ∀ k n : ℕ, 2 ≤ k → ‖∑ j ∈ range n, e (k * x j)‖ ≤ C * Real.sqrt (k * Real.log k) := by
  sorry

/- ## Question 2 -/

/-- **Question 2 (parts.ii)**: Is it possible for $A_k = o(k)$? Yes — there exists a sequence
$(x_n) \in (0, 1)$ and a bound $b(k) = o(k)$ with $A x k \le b k$ eventually. A corollary of
`sqrt_log_upper_bound` (which gives a $\sqrt{k \log k}$ bound) plus the asymptotic
$\sqrt{k \log k} = o(k)$. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11 40 42, formal_proof using lean4 at
"https://github.com/Marti2203/formal-conjectures/blob/19c63d48acce3099c242b059518c49bf8dc0eab8/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/987.lean"]
theorem erdos_987.parts.ii :
    answer(True) ↔ ∃ (x : ℕ → ℝ) (_ : ∀ j : ℕ, x j ∈ Set.Ioo (0 : ℝ) 1) (b : ℕ → ℝ),
      b =o[atTop] (fun k : ℕ => (k : ℝ)) ∧ ∀ᶠ k : ℕ in atTop, A x k ≤ ((b k : ℝ) : EReal) := by
  sorry

/-- Liu [Li69] showed that, for any $\epsilon > 0$, $A_k \gg k^{1 - \epsilon}$ infinitely often
under the additional assumption that there are only a finite number of distinct points. Clunie
observed in the Mathscinet review of [Li69] that under this assumption in fact $A_k = \infty$
infinitely often (the version stated here). -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11 40 42, formal_proof using lean4 at
"https://github.com/Marti2203/formal-conjectures/blob/19c63d48acce3099c242b059518c49bf8dc0eab8/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/987.lean"]
theorem erdos_987.variants.finite_distinct_points
    (x : ℕ → ℝ) (_hx : ∀ j : ℕ, x j ∈ Set.Ioo (0 : ℝ) 1)
    (hfin : (Set.range x).Finite) :
    ∃ᶠ k : ℕ in atTop, A x k = ⊤ := by
  sorry

end Erdos987

findings.description: The module bibliography identifies [Li69] as Bernt Lindström's “An inequality for B₂-sequences,” but `Erdos987.erdos_987.variants.finite_distinct_points` uses [Li69] for a result of Liu and Clunie's review of it. These are different papers. This is a reference error, not an error in the Lean proposition.
findings.source_evidence: The zbMATH records identify Lindström's paper as J. Combinatorial Theory 6 (1969), 211–212, concerning the maximum size of a Sidon sequence, and Ming-Chit Liu's “On a problem of Erdős” as Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 21 (1969), 706–710. Records read through https://api.zbmath.org/v1/document/_search?search_string=au%3Alindstrom%20py%3A1969%20ti%3Ainequality and https://api.zbmath.org/v1/document/_search?search_string=au%3Aliu%20py%3A1969%20ti%3Aerdos .
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the [Li69] bibliography entry with Ming-Chit Liu, “On a problem of Erdős,” Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society 21 (1969), 706–710, DOI 10.2307/2036452.

findings.description: The interval explanation in the docstring is inaccurate: it says the open-interval formulation is “strictly stronger” and attributes the half-open formulation to [Er64b]. Erdős actually uses (0,1), and the existential open- and half-open-interval bounds are equivalent by a common rotation. The Lean statement itself is legitimate; only this explanation needs correction.
findings.source_evidence: Erdős, “Problems and results on diophantine approximations,” p. 52, starts with an infinite sequence of real numbers “in the interval (0,1)” (https://www.numdam.org/item/CM_1964__16__52_0.pdf). The equivalence of the two interval formulations, preserving exactly every A_k, was proved independently in `Review987.interval_upper_iff` in the scratch file.
findings.suggested_fix: Retain either interval convention, but replace the “strictly stronger” explanation with the rotation equivalence. Do not attribute half-open interval wording to [Er64b].

findings.description: The opening docstring still asserts the unshifted √(k log k) bound for every k ≥ 1. At k = n = 1 the left side is 1 and the right side is 0, regardless of the constant. The subsequent note and the Lean declaration correctly restrict to k ≥ 2, so this is only a contradictory opening sentence.
findings.source_evidence: [APSSV26b], §3.1, states sup_{N≥1}|S_N(k)| ≪ √(k log(2k)) for every k ≥ 1, not the unshifted logarithm at k = 1. Read in the LaTeX source at https://arxiv.org/e-print/2604.06609 . The k = n = 1 obstruction was also checked in Lean.
findings.suggested_fix: Either change the opening sentence to k ≥ 2, matching the Lean, or quote the paper's √(k log(2k)) bound for k ≥ 1 and explain the equivalent normalization used below.

reformulations.difference: The exact upper-bound existence statement uses [0,1) rather than the problem's open interval (0,1).
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Given any sequence x, choose t outside the countable set {m − x_j : j ∈ ℕ, m ∈ ℤ} and put y_j = fract(x_j + t). Then every y_j lies in (0,1), and every partial sum at integer frequency k is multiplied by e(kt). Its norm, and hence A_k, is unchanged. The reverse implication follows by inclusion. The scratch theorem `interval_upper_iff` proves this for arbitrary bounds, so in particular no +1 loss is necessary for A_k ≤ k.

reformulations.difference: The source uses √(k log(2k)) for all k ≥ 1; Lean uses √(k log k) for all k ≥ 2.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The source implies the Lean bound since log(2k) ≤ 2 log k for k ≥ 2. Conversely, from a Lean witness x, take y_j = fract(2x_j + t), choosing t to avoid endpoints. The norm at frequency k for y equals that at frequency 2k for x, giving C√(2k log(2k)) for every k ≥ 1. Thus the existence statements are equivalent with an adjusted constant, although they need not use the same sequence. This ↔ is proved in `Review987.sqrt_log_exist_iff`. Including the empty partial sum is harmless.

reformulations.difference: Instead of directly writing A_k = o(k) for an extended-real-valued sequence, Lean asks for a real-valued little-o majorant that bounds A_k eventually.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: A_k is nonnegative. A real little-o majorant therefore implies that, for every ε > 0, eventually A_k ≤ εk. Conversely, these epsilon bounds make A_k finite eventually; taking b(k) = (A_k).toReal gives a real little-o sequence and the required eventual majorization. Values at finitely many exceptional indices do not affect either condition. The pointwise ↔, specialized to A, is proved in the scratch file using `littleO_majorant_iff`.

could_not_verify: Erdos987.erdos_987.variants.finite_distinct_points: I could not directly read Liu's article or Clunie's MathSciNet review to verify the precise historical attribution and source statement. Publisher/problem-page access was blocked, and the available journal-archive full text was restricted. The finite-range semantics and the bibliography mismatch were checked, but this declaration's exact correspondence to that historical remark remains unverified.
review.notes: Inspected all eleven declarations. No Lean statement defect was established; the findings concern documentation and references only. The two fixed affirmative answers and solved categories are consistent with the available literature, including APSSV26b's solution of Question 2. `/workspace/review/scratch.lean` compiles and proves the three equivalences using only standard axioms, with no `sorryAx`; it also checks boundary cases and satisfiability of the interval/finite-range hypotheses. The target file remains identical to its committed version. erdosproblems.com returned Cloudflare challenges despite descriptive User-Agent headers; published sources were used instead. External formal-proof code was not independently audited.
